strengths: Originality: The empirical observation that models inter-trained with different SSL objectives can subsequently be averaged productively is interesting. Figures 2 and 4 support this observation for MAE and Franca initializations, extending the practical recipe of model soups.

Significance: The approach preserves single-model inference cost and reports useful corruption robustness gains. In Table 2, adapting ingredients to disjoint unlabeled target samples raises ImageNet-C accuracy from 32.23% to 35.72% and LAION-C accuracy from 22.40% to 29.48%. Separating joint and disjoint adaptation settings is a valuable experimental choice.

Soundness: Tables 1 and 4 include a continued-SSL-plus-supervised-soup baseline, which helps distinguish gains from continued pretraining versus mixing across SSL runs. Evaluation spans multiple ImageNet shifts and 21 downstream tasks, and Table 3 demonstrates complementarity with SAR.

Presentation and limitations: The workflow diagrams and experimental organization make the main idea accessible. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges modest gains without target data and the restricted set of SSL algorithms. The benchmark-based study raises no apparent material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—test-set model selection: Table 4 explicitly selects both the best ingredient and greedy mixtures using clean test accuracy, then reports performance on that test set and corruptions of its images. This compromises the headline 67.5% versus 66.2% clean-transfer comparison and also exposes selection to the underlying images used for corruption evaluation. Applying this procedure to every method does not eliminate selection bias, particularly with different candidate pools. Separate validation data and untouched test evaluation are needed; uniform-mixture results remain more credible.

Soundness—attribution of the largest gains: Table 2 lacks the critical continued-SSL-plus-supervised-soup baseline inter-trained on the same shifted data with the same budget. Comparing against an ImageNet-trained soup or a single best ingredient cannot establish how much benefit comes specifically from averaging across SSL runs rather than target-distribution adaptation and ordinary supervised souping. The reported gains are promising, but the main robustness experiment does not isolate the proposed contribution.

Soundness and significance—Self-Seasoning: Appendix D minimizes entropy over neighbor identities based on feature similarities, not entropy over predicted class probabilities as the main text suggests. Its connection to classification accuracy needs justification. Table 5 shows substantial failures on structured tasks, such as CLEVR-Count falling from 33.7% for the selected ingredient to 17.5%. Averaging the reported task accuracies gives approximately 48.85% for Self-Seasoning, 51.57% for the selected ingredient, and 52.31% for supervised seasoning. Label-free selection is valuable, but the 'competitive' characterization needs qualification and comparison against simple fixed SSL-ingredient choices.

Reproducibility and statistical evidence: Appendix C contains only empty 'Data' and 'Code' headings, despite the claim that mini-VTAB-C is shared there. Exact subset indices, random seeds, important linear-probing and kNN evaluation details, and compute measurements are absent or insufficiently specified. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, which matters for the approximately 0.4–1 percentage-point improvements. The optimizer settings and entropy-function snippet help, but do not make the full evaluation reproducible.

Originality and claim scope: The contribution is primarily an empirical extension of existing inter-training and averaging recipes. Figures 2 and 4 examine models after supervised fine-tuning, so they do not establish connectivity of the raw SSL endpoints. Moreover, favorable performance at finitely sampled mixtures does not establish the all-lambda condition in Equation 1. The manuscript should distinguish sampled evidence of successful interpolation from a general connectivity claim and better isolate the effect of SSL-objective diversity from additional training or stochastic diversity.

Presentation and related-work accuracy: Section 5 incorrectly characterizes methods such as TIES-Merging as not sharing initialization and potentially differing in architecture; the cited method combines aligned task vectors from a common base. This weakens the proposed distinction between soups and merging. There are also reporting inconsistencies: Table 2 lists 79.05% for a supervised soup paired with uniform-soup corruption results, whereas Table 1 gives 79.12%, and Section 4.3 reverses the stated even/odd adaptation and evaluation indices in its TTA discussion.

strengths: Originality: Exploring parameter averaging across ingredients inter-trained with different self-supervised objectives is a useful empirical extension of model soups and Model Ratatouille. Figures 2 and 4 demonstrate beneficial mixtures after supervised fine-tuning, including results from both MAE and Franca initializations.

Significance: The approach preserves single-model inference cost. Table 2 reports substantial corruption-robustness improvements: ImageNet-C accuracy increases from 32.23% to 35.72%, and LAION-C from 22.40% to 29.48%, when ingredients receive corresponding unlabeled shifted data.

Soundness: The experiments include supervised soups, continued-SSL-plus-supervised-soup controls in Tables 1 and 4, uniform and greedy mixing, and separate joint/disjoint adaptation evaluations. Table 3 also provides evidence that the proposed adaptation can complement SAR.

Presentation and limitations: The workflow diagrams make the training stages understandable, and the evaluation spans multiple shifts and 21 downstream tasks. The limitations appropriately acknowledge modest gains outside target-distribution adaptation and dependence on access to unlabeled shifted data. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—test-set selection compromises a central transfer result. Table 4 explicitly states that both the best ingredient and greedy mixture are selected on clean test data. Consequently, the reported 67.5% versus 66.2% clean accuracy comparison is not an independent generalization evaluation. Applying this procedure to all methods does not eliminate selection bias, particularly with different candidate pools. Selection on clean versions of evaluation images also complicates interpretation of corrupted-image results. A separate validation split is needed; the uniform-mixture results remain useful but do not resolve this issue.

Soundness—the largest gains do not isolate the proposed contribution. Although Section 4 promises a continued-SSL-plus-supervised-soup baseline for Section 4.3, Table 2 only reports that baseline when inter-training uses ImageNet training data. It omits supervised soups originating from a single inter-training on the same shifted data. Comparing shifted-data Self-Soups with clean-data soups or individual shifted-data ingredients cannot establish how much improvement specifically requires mixing across SSL runs. This control is especially important because the shifted-data experiments use 100K inter-training steps, substantially more than the clean-data experiments.

Soundness—uncertainty is not quantified. Tables report no repeated-run variability or confidence intervals, despite many improvements being fractions of a percentage point and mini-VTAB using 1K-sample subsets. Evaluating 336 task/condition combinations does not substitute for repeated trials, since corruptions reuse underlying datasets and models. The reliability of the modest improvements is therefore unclear.

Soundness and significance—Self-Seasoning needs stronger validation. Appendix D minimizes entropy over similarities to neighboring instances, rather than a class-prediction distribution; the paper provides little justification for why this objective should identify mixtures with better classification accuracy. Table 5 shows substantial failures, including 17.5% versus 33.7% for the best ingredient on Clevr-Count. Many learned mixtures are nearly one-hot, making an unsupervised ingredient-selection baseline particularly relevant. Highlighting four task wins does not adequately establish the general competitiveness claimed.

Reproducibility: Appendix B supplies useful training settings and Appendix D supplies the entropy function, but Appendix C contains only empty 'Data.' and 'Code.' headings, despite the claim that mini-VTAB-C is shared there. Exact subset indices or sampling seeds, complete evaluation procedures, and the implementation are unavailable in the supplied manuscript. The supervised kNN selection protocol also does not specify whether queries are excluded from their own reference set. These omissions materially hinder reproducing the customized benchmark and selection results.

Originality and presentation: The broad claim that all previous soups require supervised learning is insufficiently substantiated, particularly given the cited language-model adaptation and pretraining literature. Section 5 also inaccurately characterizes merging methods such as TIES as methods that do not share an initialization; TIES commonly merges models fine-tuned from a shared base. The demonstrated contribution should be positioned more narrowly. Likewise, the connectivity experiments mainly concern models after a shared supervised fine-tuning stage, so their conclusions should distinguish those models from raw SSL ingredients.

strengths: Originality: Extending model soups to ingredients produced by different SSL objectives is a useful empirical contribution. Figures 2 and 4 demonstrate productive interpolation after SSL inter-training and supervised fine-tuning, including a second initialization, Franca.

Significance: The reported robustness improvements are practically interesting without increasing the deployed backbone’s inference cost. Table 2 improves ImageNet-C accuracy from 32.23% to 35.72% and LAION-C from 22.40% to 29.48% using unlabeled target-distribution data.

Soundness: The evaluation includes several ImageNet shifts and 21 downstream tasks. Separating joint and disjoint adaptation samples in Table 2 is valuable, and the continued-SSL-plus-supervised-soup baseline in Tables 1 and 4 helps distinguish SSL training from mixing across SSL runs.

Presentation and ethics: The experimental questions and diagrams make the framework accessible. The limitations appropriately acknowledge modest gains outside target adaptation and dependence on available shifted data. The impact statement recognizes computation costs; no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—test-set model selection: Table 4 explicitly states that both the best ingredient and greedy mixtures are selected on clean test data. Consequently, the highlighted 67.5% versus 66.2% clean-transfer comparison is not an independent generalization estimate. Applying this procedure to all methods does not eliminate selection bias, particularly with different candidate pools. Selection needs a separate validation set, followed by untouched clean and corrupted test evaluation.

Soundness—attribution of the largest gains: Table 2 omits the continued-SSL-plus-supervised-soup baseline trained on the same shifted data with the same training budget. Comparing with soups trained on ImageNet or with a single shifted-data ingredient does not isolate the benefit of mixing across SSL runs from target-distribution adaptation and ordinary supervised souping. This control is especially important because the largest headline gains come from this setting.

Statistical evidence: No repeated-run uncertainty is reported. Several central improvements are small: Table 1 gives 32.23% versus 31.24% on ImageNet-C, and Table 4 gives an aggregate 35.1% versus 34.6%. Multiple corruption versions of the same images are not independent replications. Seed variability and paired uncertainty estimates are needed to establish the reliability of these gains.

Self-Seasoning is insufficiently validated: Appendix D minimizes entropy over neighboring sample identities, not class-prediction entropy, and the manuscript does not establish why this objective should select task-relevant representations. Table 5 shows substantial failures, including 17.5% on Clevr-Count versus 27.4% for uniform mixing and 33.7% for the best ingredient. The coefficients frequently concentrate almost entirely on one ingredient, motivating a comparison with selecting a single ingredient by the same unlabeled entropy criterion. The distinction between label-free mixture optimization and the labeled reference set needed for kNN classification also needs clearer explanation.

Reproducibility: Appendix B supplies useful optimization settings and Appendix D supplies the entropy function, but Appendix C contains only empty 'Data' and 'Code' headings despite the claim that mini-VTAB-C is shared there. Exact subset indices, seeds, complete linear-probing settings, and the kNN training-accuracy selection protocol—including whether self-neighbors are excluded—are missing. These omissions materially hinder reproducing the custom benchmark and selection results.

Claim precision and positioning: The interpolation experiments support successful sampled mixtures under specific training recipes, rather than establishing the all-coefficients condition in Equation 1. Most also include supervised fine-tuning after SSL, so they should be distinguished from direct SSL-backbone mixing. The blanket assertion that previous soups require supervised learning needs qualification, and Section 5 inaccurately characterizes cited merging methods such as TIES as not sharing an initialization. The empirical extension has merit, but the novelty claims exceed the demonstrated scope.

strengths: Originality: Using different SSL objectives and unlabeled adaptation datasets to construct compatible soup ingredients is a useful empirical extension of model soups and Ratatouille. Self-Seasoning adds an interesting label-free objective for optimizing mixture coefficients.

Significance: The approach preserves single-model inference cost. Table 2 reports meaningful corruption-robustness improvements, and its disjoint adaptation/evaluation split is a valuable control. Comparisons against continued SSL plus supervised soups help distinguish adaptation benefits from mixing benefits.

Evaluation breadth: Experiments cover several SSL objectives, eight ImageNet evaluation sets, 21 downstream tasks with corruptions, and a second initialization. The ensemble comparisons and SAR experiment provide useful context.

Presentation and ethics: The overall workflow is understandable, and the limitations candidly acknowledge modest general gains and dependence on target-distribution data. The benchmark-based study presents no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—evaluation leakage: Table 4 explicitly selects the best ingredient and greedy mixture using clean test data, then reports clean-test accuracy. This undermines the reported 67.5% versus 66.2% transfer comparison; an independent validation set is needed. Appendix E also selects the best of six configurations on an unspecified held-out set. Its separation from final evaluation, selection criterion, and label budget must be established, particularly for the fully unsupervised Self-Seasoning claim.

Soundness—missing decisive few-shot controls: Section 4.6 compares mixtures of ingredients adapted on all target training images against fine-tuning the original stock. It omits individual adapted ingredients evaluated with the same kNN classifier and fine-tuning from those ingredients. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed to mixing rather than continued SSL and additional unlabeled data. Table 8 often assigns approximately 80–95% of the weight to one ingredient, making a single-ingredient comparison especially important.

Soundness—overstated connectivity claims: Section 4.1 infers linear mode connectivity from 64 four-model mixtures, but this does not establish Equation 1's inequality along pairwise interpolation paths. Figure 2's ImageNet-HR panel visibly contains mixtures worse than some individual ingredients, also contradicting the blanket statement that the worst models are always ingredients alone. Numerical pairwise interpolation results and a narrower statement of the finding are needed.

Significance and attribution: The headline robustness improvements combine target-distribution adaptation with souping. Against the corresponding target-adapted continued-SSL soup in Table 2, the incremental gains are 0.63 points on ImageNet-C and 2.05 points on LAION-C, rather than the headline 3.5 and 7 points. These remain useful, but the distinction should be central. Most other improvements are small, including 35.1 versus 34.6 on mini-VTAB-C, and no repeated-seed or sampling uncertainty is reported.

Reproducibility: The advertised code URL is only https://github.com/, and Appendix D's Data and Code sections are empty despite promising the custom benchmark there. Important details are missing, including mixture-coefficient parameterization and initialization, labeled kNN implementation, and precise validation splits. Equation 3 permits unrestricted coefficients while Table 8 appears to report convex weights. Appendix E also sweeps k=32 for N=25, which the supplied topk implementation cannot execute as written.

Originality and technical scope: The main construction retains standard parameter averaging and extends existing inter-training workflows. Its strongest potential contribution is therefore reliable new empirical understanding, but the missing controls and overstated connectivity conclusions weaken that contribution. The broad claim that all previous soups require supervision also needs more careful qualification and positioning against the language-model literature cited by the paper.

Presentation accuracy: Several inconsistencies impede verification: Section 4.6 points to Table 4 instead of the few-shot results; multiple table references are incorrect; Section 4.3 reverses the adaptation/evaluation indices in its SAR discussion; and Section 4.5 lists learning rates of 6e-8 and 8e-8 where other sections use 6e-5 and 8e-5. These ambiguities matter for reproducing the comparisons.

strengths: Originality: Extending model soups to ingredients produced by different self-supervised objectives is a useful empirical contribution. Mixing MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, and LeJEPA ingredients explores a meaningful source of diversity beyond supervised fine-tuning hyperparameters.

Soundness: The continued-SSL-plus-supervised-soup baseline helps distinguish continued training from mixing across SSL runs. Table 2 explicitly separates disjoint adaptation/evaluation samples from a transductive setting, and Table 3 shows that the resulting robustness gains can complement SAR adaptation.

Significance: The method produces a single backbone without ensemble inference costs. There are concrete improvements over the continued-SSL soup baseline, including 35.72 versus 35.09 on ImageNet-C and 29.48 versus 27.43 on LAION-C in Table 2. Evaluation spans multiple shifts, 21 transfer tasks, and a second initialization.

Presentation, limitations, and ethics: The pipeline diagrams make the main approach understandable. The discussion appropriately acknowledges modest general gains and dependence on unlabeled target data for the largest improvements. The standard benchmark experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—test-set model selection: Table 4 explicitly states that both the best ingredient and greedy mixtures are selected on clean test data. Consequently, the highlighted 67.5% clean accuracy is not an independent generalization estimate. Because the corrupted evaluations derive from the same underlying test images, this also compromises their separation from model selection. A distinct validation split and untouched final test set are needed.

Soundness—unclear label-free evaluation protocol: Appendix E selects the best of six Self-Seasoning configurations on a 'held-out set' without specifying whether this is a separate labeled validation set or the reported evaluation set. If selection uses labeled accuracy, the complete selection procedure is not label-free; if it uses the reported test set, there is additional test-set tuning. The paper should distinguish unsupervised coefficient optimization from hyperparameter selection and the labeled reference examples required for kNN classification.

Soundness—missing controls for Self-Seasoning: Section 4.6 compares seasoned SSL ingredients against fine-tuning the original stock, although the ingredients receive substantial additional target-domain SSL training. It does not report individual SSL ingredients evaluated with the same kNN procedure, simple ingredient selection, or fine-tuning those ingredients. Table 8 frequently assigns most weight to one ingredient, making these controls especially important: the results do not establish how much benefit comes from mixing rather than selecting a stronger adapted representation.

Significance and attribution: The headline +3.5/+7-point robustness improvements combine exposure to shifted data with averaging across SSL runs. Against the baseline that also receives shifted-data SSL, the incremental gains in Table 2 are approximately 0.63 and 2.05 points. Those remain useful, but the larger headline numbers should not be interpreted as the isolated benefit of the proposed mixing strategy. Elsewhere, improvements are often small—for example, 35.1 versus 34.6 averaged accuracy in Table 4—and no repeated-seed or uncertainty estimates establish their reliability.

Soundness and originality—connectivity claims exceed the evidence: Section 4.1 evaluates 64 mixtures after all ingredients undergo supervised fine-tuning on the same task. This supports successful averaging for that particular pipeline, but does not isolate connectivity created by SSL itself or establish Equation 1 across all interpolation coefficients. The claim that all known soups require supervision also needs more careful qualification given the discussion of language and generative-model soups. The defensible contribution is a useful empirical extension, rather than a generally established connectivity result.

Reproducibility: The abstract's code URL ends at https://github.com/, and Appendix D contains empty Data and Code subsections despite promising the mini-VTAB-C resource there. Important details remain unspecified, including subset sampling/seeds, Self-Seasoning coefficient initialization and constraints, the final kNN evaluation configuration, and complete settings for some training runs. The supplied entropy-function snippet does not reproduce the full method.

Presentation: Several inconsistencies impede verification: Sections 4.2–4.3 reference Table 7 where the quoted values correspond to Table 1; Section 4.6 references Table 4 for few-shot results; the SAR discussion reverses the even/odd adaptation split; and Section 4.5 lists learning rates of 6e-8 and 8e-8 where other sections use 6e-5 and 8e-5. These require correction, particularly where they affect experimental interpretation.

strengths: Originality: The empirical finding that models inter-trained with different SSL objectives can be usefully averaged is interesting. Experiments span reconstruction, instance-contrastive, and dimension-contrastive objectives, with an additional Franca initialization supporting applicability beyond the MAE stock.

Significance: Improving robustness without increasing the final network's inference cost is useful. Table 2 reports substantial improvements when unlabeled target-distribution data is available, and its disjoint evaluation is a valuable control against simply adapting to the evaluated samples.

Soundness: The continued-SSL-plus-supervised-soup baseline helps separate the contribution of cross-inter-training mixing from continued pretraining alone. Evaluations include multiple ImageNet shifts, 21 downstream tasks, alternative augmentations, and complementary adaptation with SAR.

Presentation and limitations: The overall workflow is understandable, and the paper candidly acknowledges modest gains outside target-distribution adaptation and weaker performance on some tasks. The benchmark-based research raises no evident material ethical concerns; the impact statement acknowledges computational costs.
weaknesses: Soundness—test-based selection: Table 4 explicitly selects the best ingredient and greedy mixture using clean test data, then reports performance on that data and its corrupted variants. This compromises the claimed transfer evaluation, particularly the highlighted 67.5% clean accuracy. Selection must use a separate validation split, followed by untouched test evaluation. Applying the same procedure to baselines does not remove selection bias when candidate pools differ.

Soundness—label-free claim: Appendix E selects the best of six Self-Seasoning configurations on an unspecified held-out set. It does not explain whether selection uses labels, whether those labels count toward the few-shot budget, or whether this set is separate from final evaluation. The coefficient objective itself is label-free, but the reported end-to-end selection protocol does not establish fully unsupervised seasoning. Labels used for the kNN reference set also need explicit accounting.

Soundness—missing decisive few-shot controls: Section 4.6 compares task-adapted SSL ingredients against fine-tuning the original stock, without reporting kNN accuracy for each individual adapted ingredient or fine-tuning the best adapted ingredient. Table 8 frequently puts 80–95% of the mixture weight on one ingredient. Consequently, the large gains over the stock and uniform soup may mainly reflect selecting a stronger representation rather than a benefit from mixing. These controls are essential to substantiate Self-Seasoning's contribution.

Significance and evidential strength: The headline adaptation improvements largely combine access to shifted data with mixing. Against the corresponding continued-SSL-plus-soup baseline in Table 2, the incremental gains are 0.63 percentage points on ImageNet-C and 2.05 on LAION-C. Elsewhere, gains are often below one point, including 35.1 versus 34.6 in Table 4. No repeated-seed or subset-sampling uncertainty is reported, making the reliability of these smaller improvements difficult to assess.

Originality and claim calibration: Figures 2 and 5 establish useful mixtures in particular experimental settings, but Section 4.1 mixes models after a shared supervised fine-tuning stage. This does not directly establish connectivity immediately after heterogeneous SSL training. Moreover, 64 sampled mixtures do not establish the universal interpolation inequality in Equation 1. The paper should distinguish observed averaging benefits from its stronger connectivity claims. Section 5 also inaccurately characterizes merging methods such as TIES as not sharing initialization; this weakens the positioning against relevant prior work.

Reproducibility and presentation: The promised repository link is only 'https://github.com/', and Appendix D contains empty Data and Code headings despite the claimed release of mini-VTAB-C. Important implementation details remain unspecified, including coefficient initialization and constraints, precise validation splits, and classification-time kNN settings. Appendix E's code also requests k=32 when some experiments have batches of only 25 samples, which requires an undocumented adjustment. Incorrect table references and inconsistent learning-rate notation further hinder reconstruction. Together with the evaluation issues above, these gaps prevent a confident acceptance recommendation.
